title: What the padlock means
description: How your browser decides a site is who it claims to be and keeps the conversation private: certificates, revocation, automated issuance, TLS and HSTS.
questions: what does the padlock in the browser mean
how does a browser verify a certificate

steps.title: A certificate says who you are
steps.subtitle: X.509
steps.description: A website proves its identity with a certificate that binds its name to a public key and is signed by a certificate authority. X.509 defines the format and how a chain of signatures is checked.

steps.title: The name must match
steps.subtitle: Service identity
steps.description: Having a valid certificate is not enough. The client also checks that the name in the certificate matches the site it meant to reach.

steps.title: Is it still good?
steps.subtitle: Revocation
steps.description: A certificate can be revoked before it expires. OCSP lets a client ask a responder about a certificate's status instead of downloading a full revocation list.

steps.title: Getting a certificate automatically
steps.subtitle: ACME
steps.description: ACME lets a server prove it controls a domain and obtain a certificate without a human, which is what made short-lived certificates and free HTTPS practical.

steps.title: Encrypt the connection
steps.subtitle: TLS 1.3
steps.description: TLS agrees on keys, authenticates the server and encrypts everything that follows. TLS 1.3 was published as RFC 8446 and has since been revised as RFC 9846; the older TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated.

steps.title: Never fall back to plain HTTP
steps.subtitle: HSTS and https
steps.description: A site can tell browsers to use only HTTPS for it from now on. The padlock also depends on how HTTP defines the https scheme.
